Pure CSS · no JavaScript · no WebGL

Ray tracing in a stylesheet

Three spheres, a checkerboard floor, soft shadows, ambient occlusion and a mirror reflection. Every pixel is an <i> element whose color comes out of sqrt(), pow(), exp(), hypot(), sign() and sibling-index().

This browser does not support sibling-index(). Open the page in Chrome or Edge 138 or later to see the render.

Display

Every change clears the image and redraws it one scanline at a time, top to bottom, like a 1980 renderer.

What the browser is computing

There is no script on this page. Each pixel is an <i> element with 75 properties registered through @property. The style engine resolves them as a chain of numeric expressions, and the last one becomes the element's background-color.

  1. Pixel coordinates

    sibling-index() and sibling-count() tell each element where it sits in its row and how many rows there are. That gives the direction of the ray leaving the camera.

    --u: calc((2 * sibling-index() - 1 - sibling-count()) / var(--hh));
--rl: hypot(var(--rx), var(--qy), var(--rz));

  2. Sphere intersections

    The ray against each sphere is a quadratic with a discriminant. When the discriminant is negative, sign() adds 100,000 to the distance and that sphere loses the min() that follows. That is how the stylesheet branches without if.

    --e0: calc(sqrt(max(var(--b0) * var(--b0) - var(--c0), 0)) * -1 - var(--b0)
      + 1e5 * max(0, sign(var(--c0) - var(--b0) * var(--b0))));
--tm: min(var(--e0), var(--e1), var(--e2), var(--ef));

  3. Soft shadows and occlusion

    For each sphere, the closest approach between the sun ray and the sphere center gives a penumbra that widens with distance. Floor occlusion uses the analytic solid-angle formula, with pow(d², 1.5).

    --s1: max(clamp(0, (sqrt(max(var(--a1) - pow(var(--l1) - var(--pl), 2), 0)) - .55)
      / max(var(--l1) - var(--pl), 1e-4) * var(--soft), 1), sign(var(--pl) - var(--l1)));

  4. Second ray: the reflection

    At the hit point, m = d − 2(d·n)n gives the reflected ray, which is tested again against the three spheres and the floor. The center sphere shows the checkerboard, the other spheres and the sun; the floor reflects the sky following Fresnel, with pow(1 − |d·n|, 5). Fog uses exp().

    --fo: calc(1 - var(--if) * (1 - exp(-.07 * max(0, var(--tm) - 7))));

  5. Scanline scheduler

    Computing all 5,184 pixels at once would freeze the tab for seconds. Every row starts as display: none, held there by 1 ms animations whose delay grows with the row index. While a row is hidden, the browser computes none of its pixels. Each control group owns one animation in the list, and :has() swaps its name when you pick an option. A new name restarts the animation, the rows disappear, and the image comes back from the top.

    animation-name: var(--a-cam), var(--a-hgt), var(--a-sun), var(--a-mat), var(--a-pas), …;
animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * var(--step) + 120ms);

.app:has(#m1:checked) .fb > b { --mr: .12; --mg: .07; …; --a-mat: rv-mat-m1 }
@keyframes rv-mat-m1 { from, to { display: none } }

The scene is a tribute to Turner Whitted's 1980 image, the first to trace recursive reflections: spheres over a red and yellow checkerboard. It runs in Chrome and Edge 138 or later, which shipped sibling-index(), sign() and abs(). On a 2.8 GHz Xeon each pixel cost about 0.7 ms of style work, so the scheduler budgets 0.72 ms per pixel: 69 ms per scanline at 96×54, about 4 seconds per frame.
